decks.title: Introduction to Accounting, Part 1: History, the accounting cycle and basic terms
goals: Outline how accounting developed from early records to modern practice
Distinguish book-keeping, accounting and accountancy, and order the stages of the accounting cycle
Distinguish an event from a transaction, and explain voucher, capital and drawings
Separate expense from loss, revenue from income, and profit from gain

slides.heading: Where accounting begins
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **story** of accounting, its **cycle** and the **basic terms** used in every book.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: history, three terms, the accounting cycle and basic terms
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every shop, workshop and company has to know what it earns, what it owes and what it owns. Accounting gives the answers. In this part we see how it grew, how its work is organised and the basic words that every later chapter depends on.

slides.heading: A brief history of accounting

visual.alt: Five stages in the development of accounting: early records, growth of trade and credit, double entry, factories and companies, and standards and computers
visual.caption: From tallies to computers

slides.narration: People kept records long before modern business. Early rulers and traders noted stores, taxes and debts on tablets, leaves and tallies. As trade grew, merchants developed double entry in the Italian trading cities. Factories and companies brought cost records and yearly statements, and today standards and computers shape the work.

slides.heading: What each stage needed

rows: To remember stores, taxes and debts
Tallies, clay tablets, palm leaves and scribes' lists
To track purchases, sales and credit
Merchants' books, including the bahi-khata of Indian traders
Each transaction recorded twice; described in print in the late fifteenth century
Cost facts and reports for owners far away
Cost records, yearly statements and audit

visual.alt: Table of five stages in the history of accounting with what people needed and what developed

slides.narration: Each step in the history met a new need. Early records helped people remember. Trade between towns needed books of purchases, sales and credit, such as the bahi khata of Indian traders. Double entry let a merchant check that his records agreed. Companies needed reports for owners far away. No exact dates are needed here.

slides.heading: Book-keeping, accounting and accountancy

rows: Recording and classifying transactions in the books
Entering each credit sale and sorting it under the customer's name
The process that summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the records
Finding that profit fell and telling the owner why
The body of principles, rules and techniques behind the work
The rule that every transaction has a two-fold effect

visual.alt: Table comparing book-keeping, accounting and accountancy by meaning and example

slides.narration: These three words are often mixed up. Book-keeping is the recording and classifying of transactions. Accounting is wider. It starts from those records, then summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates them. Accountancy is the body of principles and techniques, the theory, which guides the practice.

visual.alt: Six stages of the accounting cycle in order: identify and measure, record in the journal, classify in the ledger, summarise in the trial balance and statements, analyse and interpret, and communicate to the users
visual.caption: The accounting cycle.

slides.narration: The work of accounting follows six stages. A transaction is identified and measured in money. It is recorded in the journal, classified in the ledger, and summarised in the trial balance and statements. The figures are then analysed and interpreted, and finally communicated to the people who need them.

slides.heading: Quick check: order the cycle
slides.body_md: Arrange the stages of the accounting cycle in the right order.
slides.narration: Begin with the stage where the transaction is first noticed and measured, and end with the stage where users receive the information.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which stage?
slides.body_md: Sirsa Handloom Stores is an imagined shop. Name the stage of the cycle that each activity belongs to.

rows: Her helper notes that a bulk order has been placed and that it can be written in money
Each bill is written in the day book in date order
Entries are sorted into accounts such as Sales, Rent and each customer
A trial balance and the year-end statements are prepared
She finds that wages have grown faster than sales and asks why
The statements are sent to the bank for a loan request

visual.alt: Worked example table matching six activities at Sirsa Handloom Stores to the stages of the accounting cycle
visual.caption: Ask what each activity produces.

slides.narration: Noticing a bulk order that can be written in money is identifying. Writing each bill in the day book is recording. Sorting entries into accounts is classifying. Preparing the trial balance and statements is summarising. Asking why wages grew faster than sales is analysing and interpreting. Sending statements to the bank is communicating.

slides.heading: Event and transaction

rows: Anything that happens in or around the business
A customer asks for a price list
An event that can be measured in money and changes the finances of the firm
Money is paid or received at once
Paying the day's wages in cash
Value passes now and the payment follows later
Buying goods payable after a month

visual.alt: Table of event, transaction, cash transaction and credit transaction with meanings and examples

slides.narration: An event is anything that happens in or around the business. A transaction is an event that can be measured in money and changes the finances of the firm. A cash transaction is settled at once. In a credit transaction, value passes now and payment follows later.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: event or transaction?
slides.body_md: Nagaon Silk Cocoons is an imagined firm. Classify each happening and give the reason.

rows: A weaver telephones to ask the price of cocoons
No money value has been exchanged
The owner decides to hire a supervisor from next month
Nothing has been paid or promised in money yet
Cocoons of ₹90,000 are bought from a farm group, payment due in 30 days
Silk yarn is sold for ₹45,000 and the money is taken at once
The electricity bill of ₹6,500 is paid
Payment made for a service used
A buyer gives ₹20,000 in advance for a future order
Money received, goods to be sent later

visual.alt: Worked example table of six happenings at Nagaon Silk Cocoons, each classified as an event only, a cash transaction or a credit transaction with the reason

slides.narration: A weaver asking a price has exchanged nothing, so it is an event only. Deciding to hire a supervisor involves no money yet, so it is also only an event. Buying cocoons payable in thirty days is a credit transaction. Selling yarn for cash, paying the electricity bill and taking an advance are cash transactions.

slides.heading: Quick check: a transaction
slides.body_md: Which happening at an imagined kite shop is a business transaction?
slides.narration: Look for an exchange of value that can be measured in money.

slides.heading: Voucher: the proof of a transaction

rows: Receipt of money from a customer
Cheque counterfoil and the payee's receipt

visual.alt: Table of transactions and the voucher that is evidence of each

slides.narration: Every entry in the books should rest on a voucher, which is documentary evidence of the transaction. A sale for cash has a cash memo. A credit purchase has the supplier's invoice. Money received has a receipt. A cheque payment has a counterfoil and the payee's receipt. A return of goods may have a credit note.

slides.heading: Capital and drawings

rows: What the owner has put in, with profits left in the firm
It is the owner's claim; also called an internal liability
Cash or goods taken out for the owner's own use

visual.alt: Table of capital and drawings with meaning and effect on the owner's claim

slides.narration: Capital is what the owner has put into the business, together with profits left in it. It is the owner's claim and is called an internal liability. Drawings are cash or goods the owner takes out for personal use. They reduce capital, and they are not an expense of the business.

slides.heading: Expense and loss

rows: Fall in capital with nothing received in return
The firm gets service or use for it
Goods stolen, goods spoiled by a flood

visual.alt: Table comparing expense and loss by meaning, nature, benefit and example

slides.narration: An expense is a cost incurred to earn revenue, and the firm gets service or use in return. Wages, rent and advertising are examples. A loss is a fall in capital for which nothing comes back, and it is usually unusual or accidental, such as goods stolen or spoiled by a flood.

slides.heading: Revenue and income

rows: Earnings from the main activity of the firm
Revenue together with other earnings and gains
Sales of goods; fees for services

visual.alt: Table comparing revenue and income by meaning, example and width

slides.narration: Revenue means earnings from the main activity of the firm, such as the sale of goods or fees for services. Income is the wider term. It includes revenue and also other earnings such as interest received and commission earned, along with gains.

slides.heading: Profit and gain

rows: Income less expenses of a period
Selling price of an asset above its book value
Old machine sold above its book value

visual.alt: Table comparing profit and gain by source, measure and example

slides.narration: Profit is the surplus of income over expenses from the normal activity in a period. A gain comes from an incidental or occasional event, for example selling an old machine for more than its book value. The firm does not deal in machines, so this is not part of its trading revenue.

slides.heading: Quick check: a gain
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about selling an old almirah above its book value is true or false.
slides.narration: Ask whether the almirah is what the trader sells in the ordinary course of business.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: profit of a firm
slides.body_md: Raichur Cotton Ginners is an imagined firm. Find the profit, then the net profit after a gain and a loss.

headers: Raichur Cotton Ginners for the year (imagined)
rows: Add: gain on an old ginning press

visual.alt: Worked example table of the profit of Raichur Cotton Ginners from revenue and other income less expenses, then adjusted for a gain and a loss to a net profit
visual.caption: Profit is income less expenses.

slides.narration: Revenue is net sales of rupees nine lakh thirty thousand. Adding interest and commission gives total income of rupees nine lakh sixty six thousand. Expenses come to rupees seven lakh ninety six thousand, so profit is rupees one lakh seventy thousand. The gain of rupees six thousand five hundred on an old press is added and the loss of rupees eight thousand by theft is deducted, giving net profit of rupees one lakh sixty eight thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: capital of the firm
slides.body_md: Carry the net profit of Raichur Cotton Ginners into its capital account.

visual.alt: Worked example table of capital of Raichur Cotton Ginners from opening capital plus capital introduced plus net profit less drawings to closing capital

slides.narration: Opening capital is rupees five lakh twenty thousand. The owner puts in rupees fifty thousand more, and the net profit of rupees one lakh sixty eight thousand five hundred is added. Drawings of rupees seventy two thousand are deducted. Closing capital is therefore rupees six lakh sixty six thousand five hundred.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Records, trade, double entry, factories and companies, standards and computers
Book-keeping records; accounting interprets and communicates; accountancy is the body of principles
Identify, record, classify, summarise, analyse and interpret, communicate
Expense, loss; revenue, income; profit, gain

visual.alt: Summary table of deck 1: history, three terms, accounting cycle, basic terms and results

slides.narration: In short. Accounting grew from early records, through trade and double entry, to companies and computers. Book-keeping records, accounting interprets and communicates, and accountancy is the body of principles. The cycle has six stages. A transaction is an event measurable in money. Expense differs from loss, revenue from income, and profit from gain.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1

rows: Accountancy is the work of writing the books
That is book-keeping; accountancy is the body of principles
Drawings reduce capital and are not an expense
Only events measurable in money that change the finances are transactions
An expense earns revenue; a loss gives nothing in return

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in deck 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: Do not call accountancy the work of writing the books. Never treat drawings as an expense. Remember that only events measurable in money are transactions. In a distinction question, write two points for each term and add an example. Keep the stages of the cycle in order.

visual.caption: Kinds of assets.

slides.narration: An asset is a resource the firm owns from which it expects future benefit. Fixed assets are held for use over many years and may be tangible, intangible or wasting. Current assets, such as stock and debtors, turn into cash within a year. Liquid assets are cash and bank. Fictitious assets are expenses not yet written off.

slides.heading: Fixed assets

rows: Has physical form and is used over many years
No physical form but has value to the firm

visual.alt: Table of tangible and intangible fixed assets with meaning and examples

slides.narration: Tangible fixed assets can be seen and touched, such as land, buildings, plant and furniture. Intangible fixed assets have no physical form but have value to the firm, such as a patent, a trademark, a copyright or goodwill. Both are used over many years and not bought for resale.

slides.heading: Current and liquid assets

rows: Held for sale or likely to turn into cash within a year
Cash or what turns into cash almost at once without loss
Cash in hand, bank balance, marketable securities

visual.alt: Table of current assets and liquid assets with meaning and examples

slides.narration: A current asset is held for sale or likely to turn into cash within a year. Stock, debtors, cash and bank balances are examples. A liquid asset is one that is cash already, or turns into cash almost at once without loss, such as cash in hand, a bank balance or marketable securities.

slides.heading: Wasting and fictitious assets

rows: A real asset used up as it is worked
Not a real asset: an expense not yet written off, with no resale value

visual.alt: Table of wasting and fictitious assets with meaning and examples

slides.narration: A wasting asset is a real asset that is used up as it is worked, such as a quarry, a mine or an oil well. A fictitious asset is not real at all. It is an expense, such as preliminary expenses, that has not yet been written off and has no resale value.

sections.heading: 1. History; book-keeping, accounting and accountancy
sections.body_md:
Records of stores, taxes and debts were kept in ancient times on tallies, tablets and leaves. As trade between towns grew, merchants needed records of credit; in the Italian trading cities they developed **double entry**, described in print in the late fifteenth century, and Indian traders kept the bahi-khata. Factories and joint-stock companies later called for cost records, yearly statements and audit, and today **accounting standards** and **computerised accounting** guide the work.

**Book-keeping** is recording and classifying; **accounting** goes on to summarise, analyse, interpret and communicate; **accountancy** is the body of principles that guides both.

The process that starts from the records and ends with reports and advice for users.
The theory: the principles, rules and techniques on which accounting practice rests.
The system under which each transaction is recorded in two accounts.

sections.heading: 3. Events, transactions, vouchers, capital and drawings
sections.body_md:
An **event** is anything that happens; a **transaction** is an event measurable in money that changes the finances of the firm. It may be a **cash** or a **credit** transaction. A **voucher** is the written proof: a cash memo, an invoice, a receipt.

**Capital** is the owner's investment with profits left in the firm; **drawings** are cash or goods taken for personal use and reduce capital.

Closing capital = opening capital + capital introduced + net profit − drawings. For Raichur Cotton Ginners (imagined): ₹5,20,000 + ₹50,000 + ₹1,68,500 − ₹72,000 = ₹6,66,500.

sections.heading: 4. Expense, loss, revenue, income, profit and gain
sections.body_md:
An **expense** is incurred to earn revenue; a **loss** is a fall in capital that returns nothing. **Revenue** comes from the main activity; **income** is wider and includes other earnings and gains. **Profit** is the surplus of income over expenses from normal activity; a **gain** arises from an incidental event, such as selling an old asset above its book value.

Profit = income − expenses. Net profit after incidental items = profit + gains − losses. For Raichur Cotton Ginners (imagined): ₹9,66,000 − ₹7,96,000 = ₹1,70,000; net profit ₹1,68,500.

*Books differ slightly in how they split revenue and income; use the definitions given here and state both parts of a distinction.*

Earnings from the main business activity, such as sales.

The excess of income over expenses in an accounting period.

sections.heading: 5. Assets
sections.body_md:
An **asset** is a resource owned by the firm from which future benefit is expected.

- **Fixed assets:** held for use over many years; **tangible** (land, plant) or **intangible** (patent, goodwill); a **wasting** asset (quarry, mine) is used up as it is worked.
- **Current assets:** stock, debtors, cash and bank, held for sale or likely to become cash within a year; **liquid assets** are cash or what turns into cash at once (some books also count debtors and bills receivable).
- **Fictitious assets:** expenses not yet written off, with no resale value, such as preliminary expenses.

A fixed asset with value but no physical form.
Cash or an asset that turns into cash almost immediately with no loss.
A real asset that diminishes as it is worked.
An expense carried forward that is not a real asset.

sections.heading: 6. Liabilities and the capital equation
sections.body_md:
A **liability** is an amount the business has to meet. **Internal:** capital, owed to the owner. **External:** owed to outsiders, **current** (due within a year) or **long-term** (due later). A **contingent liability** depends on an uncertain future event, such as a pending claim, so it is noted and **not** recorded as an actual liability.

**Capital = assets − external liabilities.** Tezu Lemon Squash Works (imagined): ₹7,09,000 − ₹3,20,000 = ₹3,89,000; the ₹25,000 court claim is left out. Bhuj Embroidery House (imagined): ₹9,25,000 − ₹3,41,000 = ₹5,84,000.

key_terms.definition_md: An amount which the business is bound to pay.
An external liability due within one year, such as creditors.
An external liability due after one year, such as a long loan.
A possible obligation that arises only if a future event occurs.

sections.heading: 7. Trade terms and stock
sections.body_md:
**Goods** are what the firm buys to resell or to make into what it sells; **purchases** and **sales** may each be for cash or on credit. A **trade debtor** owes the firm for goods sold on credit; a **trade creditor** is owed for goods bought on credit. A supplier of a machine on credit is a creditor for an asset, not a trade creditor.

A manufacturer holds **raw material**, **work in progress** (partly made) and **finished goods**. **Opening stock** is the stock at the start of a period; **closing stock** is the stock at the end, carried forward as the next opening stock.

Closing stock = opening stock + net purchases − cost of goods sold. Pathankot Hosiery (imagined): ₹85,000 + ₹6,15,000 − ₹6,18,000 = ₹82,000.

key_terms.definition_md: A customer who has bought goods on credit and still owes for them.
A supplier who has sold goods on credit and is still to be paid.
Stock waiting to enter the process of making goods.
Stock that is partly made and not yet ready for sale.
Complete goods that are ready for sale.
The stock at the end of a period; it is the next period's opening stock.

sections.heading: 8. Users of accounting information; financial, cost and management accounting
sections.body_md:
**Internal users:** owners (profit, safety of capital), managers (detailed facts to plan and control), employees (wages, bonus, job security). **External users:** lenders and banks (ability to repay), investors (return and risk), suppliers on credit (ability to pay), government and tax authorities (profit for tax), customers and the public.

**Financial accounting** reports the profit and position of the whole firm, chiefly to owners and outsiders. **Cost accounting** finds the cost of products, jobs and services. **Management accounting** supplies managers with information to plan, control and decide, looking forward as well as back.

key_terms.definition_md: A user who owns, manages or works in the business.
A user outside the business who deals with it or has an interest in it.
The branch that reports the results and position of the whole firm.
The branch concerned with finding and controlling costs.
The branch that gives managers the information they need to decide.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded.** Definitions and distinctions earn a mark for each side; write a point for both terms and add an example. A classification item earns a mark for each correct class; an amount item earns a mark for the method (the equation) and a mark for the answer. Show assets and liabilities as lists, then the equation, then the result, as a short table.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling accountancy the work of writing the books: that is book-keeping.
- Treating drawings as an expense: they reduce capital.
- Treating every event as a transaction: it must be measurable in money.
- Writing that a loss is an expense, or that a gain is part of trading revenue.
- Deducting a contingent liability from assets to find capital.
- Calling the seller of a machine on credit a trade creditor.
- Describing work in progress as finished goods.

**Tips:** keep the six stages of the cycle in order; give the exact class when classifying; say whether a user is inside or outside the firm; name the user and the need together.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the history of accounting is correct?

options.text_md: Double entry was first used only after computers came into business
Merchants of the Italian trading cities developed double entry, and a printed account of it appeared in the late fifteenth century
Written records were kept only by joint-stock companies, never by ancient rulers or traders
Cost accounting is older than any form of record keeping

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Merchants of the Italian trading cities developed double entry, and a printed account of it appeared in the late fifteenth century. Early records of stores, taxes and trade were kept long before double entry. Double entry grew out of expanding trade in medieval Italy, which is why a computer-era origin or an origin in companies alone is wrong, and cost accounting came much later with factories.

questions.stem_md: A commerce student writes: "The principles, concepts and conventions that guide how the books are kept form a body of knowledge." Which term does this describe?

options.text_md: Book-keeping
Auditing
Costing
Accountancy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Accountancy. Accountancy is the theory behind the practice. Book-keeping only records and sorts, auditing is an independent check of the books, and costing deals with the cost of products.

questions.stem_md: Mohan runs an imagined pickle business in Kullu. At the end of the month he prepares a trial balance and a statement of profit from the ledger balances. Which stage of the accounting cycle is this?

options.text_md: Summarising
Classifying
Recording
Communicating

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Summarising. Bringing the ledger balances together into a trial balance and statements is summarising. Sorting entries under account heads is classifying, writing the first entry is recording, and sending the statements to a user is communicating.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Book-keeping is often called the base on which accounting rests.

**Reason (R):** The records that a book-keeper prepares are the starting material that accounting summarises, analyses and interprets.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true. Accounting cannot summarise or interpret anything that has not first been recorded and sorted, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.stem_md: Accountancy means the actual work of entering each day's transactions in the books.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** That work is book-keeping. Accountancy is the body of principles and techniques, the knowledge, on which accounting practice is based.

questions.stem_md: The stage of the accounting cycle in which entries of the same kind are grouped under heads such as Sales, Rent and a customer's name is called ___.
questions.solution_md: Grouping entries under account heads is the stage of classifying, which is done in the ledger.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages of the accounting cycle in the correct order, from the first to the last.

options.text_md: Communicating
Classifying
Recording
Analysing and interpreting
Identifying and measuring
Summarising

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). A transaction is first identified and measured in money, then recorded, then classified, then summarised, then analysed and interpreted, and finally communicated to the users.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State **two** points of difference between book-keeping and accounting.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid differences, each stated for both terms, earn a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Scope:** book-keeping stops at recording and classifying transactions; accounting goes on to summarise, analyse, interpret and communicate them.
2. **Skill and purpose:** book-keeping needs care and accuracy in routine work and gives clean records; accounting needs knowledge and judgement and gives information for decisions.

marking_scheme.step: First point of difference stated for both terms
Second point of difference stated for both terms

questions.stem_md: Give **two** developments that made accounting more important and more detailed over time.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each development with its effect; no dates are needed.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Growth of trade and credit:** when merchants bought and sold on credit across towns, they needed lasting records of what was owed and by whom, which led to double entry.
2. **Factories and companies:** large factories and companies with many shareholders needed cost records, regular statements and checks by outsiders, and later computers made the work faster.

marking_scheme.step: First development with its effect on accounting
Second development with its effect on accounting

questions.stem_md: Explain the stages of **classifying** and **summarising** in the accounting cycle.
questions.solution_md: A mark for each stage explained with the place or product of the work.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Classifying:** the recorded entries are sorted and grouped under account heads, such as one account for Sales and one for each customer, usually in the ledger.
2. **Summarising:** the balances of the accounts are brought together into a trial balance and then into the final statements showing profit or loss and the financial position.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish **book-keeping**, **accounting** and **accountancy** in one or two lines each.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each term, correctly separated from the other two.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Book-keeping** is the work of recording transactions in the books and classifying them under heads.
2. **Accounting** is the wider process that starts from these records and summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the results to users.
3. **Accountancy** is the body of principles, concepts and techniques, the theory, which guides how accounting is practised.

Sirsa Handloom Stores (imagined) does the following three things. Name the stage of the accounting cycle that each one belongs to.

| (a) Each bill is written in the day book in date order | ? |
| (b) A trial balance and the year-end statements are prepared | ? |
| (c) The statements are sent to the bank for a loan request | ? |
questions.solution_md: Ask what the work produces: an entry, a group of entries, a statement or a delivery to a user.

questions.stem_md:
Kullu Pickle Pantry (imagined) sells pickles worth ₹7,200 on credit to a hotel.

(a) Name the six stages of the accounting cycle in order. [2]

(b) For this sale, say what is done at the stages of recording, classifying and summarising. [3]
questions.solution_md: Marks go to the correct order, and then one mark for each of the three stages applied to the sale.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The stages are: identifying and measuring; recording; classifying; summarising; analysing and interpreting; communicating.
**(b)** The sale of ₹7,200 is identified as a credit sale and measured in rupees.
- **Recording:** a bill is raised and the sale is entered in the book of original entry in date order.
- **Classifying:** the entry is posted to the Sales account and to the hotel's personal account, so that all sales and all dues from the hotel can be seen together.
- **Summarising:** at the month end the balances, including the hotel's dues, are brought into a trial balance and then into the statements.

marking_scheme.step: Stages named in the right order (two marks if all six are right, one if at most one is misplaced)

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a business transaction of Lohit Kites (an imagined shop)?

options.text_md: A customer asks whether a discount will be given on a bulk order next season
The owner thinks of opening a second shop in the town
It sells kites worth ₹6,000 and receives the money at once
A school writes to say it may place an order after the holidays

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It sells kites worth ₹6,000 and receives the money at once. A transaction needs an exchange of value that can be measured in money. A request about a discount, a plan to open a shop and a possible order are events: nothing has been exchanged yet.

questions.stem_md: A cash memo, a receipt or a supplier's bill that is kept as proof of an entry in the books is called a

options.text_md: ledger
trial balance
voucher
journal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** voucher. A voucher is the documentary evidence of a transaction. A journal and a ledger are books, and a trial balance is a list of balances.

questions.stem_md: Shruti Sweets (imagined) buys sugar worth ₹18,000 and agrees to pay for it after twenty days. What kind of transaction is this?

options.text_md: A credit transaction
A cash transaction
An event that is not a transaction
Drawings by the owner

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A credit transaction. Value has been received but the payment is postponed, so it is a credit transaction. It is not a cash transaction because no money changes hands now, and it is a transaction, not a mere event, because it is measurable in money.

questions.stem_md: Ritwik, who owns an imagined hardware shop, takes goods that cost ₹4,500 to use at his home. What is the effect on the business?

options.text_md: Expenses rise by ₹4,500, so profit falls by the same amount
Sales rise by ₹4,500, because the goods have left the shop
There is no effect, because the goods stayed in the owner's own family
The owner's capital falls by ₹4,500, because these are drawings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The owner's capital falls by ₹4,500, because these are drawings. Goods taken for personal use are drawings. They reduce capital and are not an expense, so profit is not reduced. They are not a sale because no customer paid, and the claim that nothing changes ignores the separate existence of the business from its owner.

questions.stem_md: Which one of these is a loss of a business and not an expense?

options.text_md: Wages paid to the shop assistant for the month
Goods worth ₹5,000 stolen from the godown and not insured
Rent paid for the shop premises
Advertising charges paid to a local newspaper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Goods worth ₹5,000 stolen from the godown and not insured. Theft reduces capital without any benefit coming back to the firm, and it is not incurred to earn revenue, so it is a loss. Wages, rent and advertising are costs incurred in earning revenue, so they are expenses.

questions.stem_md: For a firm that trades in goods, which item is income but is not revenue from its main activity?

options.text_md: Interest received on a fixed deposit with a bank
Cash sales of goods in the shop
Credit sales of goods to a dealer
Sales made through the firm's website

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Interest received on a fixed deposit with a bank. Revenue arises from selling goods in the main activity, whether for cash, on credit or online. Interest on a deposit is an earning from outside that activity, so it is income without being revenue.

questions.stem_md: Bhadra Courier Services (imagined) sells an old delivery van whose book value is ₹52,000 for ₹58,500. How should the difference be described?

options.text_md: A profit of ₹58,500, the full sale price
A gain of ₹6,500, arising from an incidental event
A loss of ₹6,500
An expense of ₹52,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A gain of ₹6,500, arising from an incidental event. The van is not what the firm sells, so the excess over book value is incidental. It equals ₹58,500 − ₹52,000 = ₹6,500. Treating the whole price as profit ignores book value, a loss would need a price below book value, and a sale is not an expense.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Drawings reduce the capital of a sole proprietor.

**Reason (R):** Capital is the amount which the owner has invested in the business, together with profits left in it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but the reason only defines capital. It does not say why drawings reduce it: drawings reduce capital because the owner takes value out of the business.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Goods destroyed in a flood are a loss to the business and not an expense.

**Reason (R):** A loss always brings the firm some benefit in return for the amount lost.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: the flood reduces capital without any purpose of earning revenue. The reason is false, because a loss is exactly the fall in capital for which nothing is received.

questions.stem_md: Cash which the owner of a shop withdraws for household use is an expense of the shop, because the money leaves the business.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It is drawings, which reduce capital. An expense is incurred to earn revenue, and a household withdrawal earns none.

questions.stem_md: A trader who sells an old almirah for more than its book value has made a gain, which does not form part of the revenue from selling the goods the trader deals in.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The excess arises from an incidental event, not from the regular trading activity, so it is a gain and not part of revenue.

questions.stem_md: The capital of a sole proprietor equals total assets minus ___ liabilities.
questions.solution_md: Capital is the owner's claim, so it is found after deducting external liabilities, those owed to outsiders.

questions.stem_md: Chandra Candle Works (imagined) had sales of ₹4,20,000 with sales returns of ₹15,000 and earned commission of ₹9,000 during the year. Its cost of goods sold was ₹2,70,000, wages ₹48,000, rent ₹24,000 and interest paid ₹6,000. Find its profit for the year.

Gurpreet owns an imagined tyre shop. His capital at the start of the year was ₹3,60,000. During the year he put in a further ₹25,000, the shop earned a profit of ₹84,000 and he withdrew ₹45,000 for personal use. Find the capital at the end of the year.

Barpeta Bamboo Mats (imagined) paid wages of ₹36,000, rent of ₹18,000 and advertising of ₹6,500. It lost goods worth ₹12,000 in a flood and ₹4,000 by theft, and the owner took ₹9,000 for household use. Find the total expenses of the business.
questions.solution_md: Only costs incurred to earn revenue are expenses; the two losses and the household withdrawal are left out. Expenses = 36,000 + 18,000 + 6,500 = ₹60,500.

questions.stem_md: Sonal runs an imagined bakery school. Her capital was ₹4,20,000 at the start of the year and ₹5,10,000 at the end. She put in no new capital and withdrew ₹30,000 for personal use. Find the profit of the year.
questions.solution_md: Closing capital = opening capital + profit − drawings, so profit = 5,10,000 − 4,20,000 + 30,000 = ₹1,20,000.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish an **expense** from a **loss**, giving one example of each.
questions.solution_md: A mark for the difference in the benefit received, and a mark for the correct examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. An **expense** is a cost incurred in the ordinary course of earning revenue, and the firm gets a benefit for it; for example, shop rent.
2. A **loss** is a fall in capital that arises from an unusual or accidental event and brings no benefit in return; for example, goods stolen from the godown.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between **revenue** and **income**, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Revenue is the narrower term. Credit the example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Revenue** is the amount earned from the main activity of the business, such as the sale of goods or fees for services.
2. **Income** is the wider term: it includes revenue and also other earnings, such as interest and commission received and gains.

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between **profit** and **gain**. A trader sells an old computer, book value ₹14,000, for ₹16,500: find the gain.
questions.solution_md: Two marks for the distinction and one for the computed gain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Profit** is the excess of income over expenses from the normal activity of the business in a period.
2. **Gain** is an increase in capital from an incidental or occasional event, outside the regular activity of the business.
3. Gain on the computer = ₹16,500 − ₹14,000 = ₹2,500.

marking_scheme.step: Gain explained as incidental or occasional

questions.stem_md: Define **drawings**. Then find the closing capital of Yamini, who owns an imagined sewing school, from these facts: opening capital ₹2,80,000, capital introduced ₹40,000, profit for the year ₹62,000 and cash drawn for household use ₹36,000.
questions.solution_md: A mark for the definition, one for the additions and one for the closing figure.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Drawings** are cash or goods taken out of the business by the owner for personal use; they reduce capital and are not an expense.

| Capital account | ₹ |

| Opening capital | 2,80,000 |
| Add: capital introduced | 40,000 |
| Add: profit | 62,000 |

questions.stem_md:
Distinguish between the following pairs, with one example of each term: [5]

(a) expense and loss [2]

(b) revenue and income [1]

(c) profit and gain [2]
questions.solution_md: One mark for each side of (a) and (c), and one mark in (b) for both terms with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** An expense is incurred to earn revenue and returns a benefit, for example wages. A loss lowers capital by accident or through an unusual event and returns nothing, for example goods lost in a fire.

**(b)** Revenue comes from the main activity, for example sale of goods. Income includes revenue and other earnings, for example interest received.

**(c)** Profit is the surplus of income over expenses of a period from the regular activity. A gain comes from an incidental event, for example selling an old machine above its book value.

marking_scheme.step: (b) revenue and income distinguished with an example

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an intangible fixed asset of a firm?

options.text_md: A delivery van
Goods kept for sale
The copyright of a training manual which the firm has published
Cash at the bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The copyright of a training manual which the firm has published. A copyright has value to the firm but no physical form, and it is used over many years. The van is a tangible fixed asset, and the goods and the bank balance are current assets.

questions.stem_md: Pench Stone Quarries (imagined) leases a hillside from which it cuts stone for sale. The value of the leased quarry falls as the stone is removed. This is an example of a

options.text_md: fictitious asset
liquid asset
contingent asset
wasting asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** wasting asset. A wasting asset is gradually used up as it is exploited, like a quarry or a mine. A fictitious asset is an unwritten-off expense, and a liquid asset is cash or something that turns into cash almost at once.

questions.stem_md: Which item is shown as a fictitious asset until it is written off?

options.text_md: Goodwill bought from a former owner
A registered patent
Furniture bought for the office
Cost of forming the business that has not yet been written off

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cost of forming the business that has not yet been written off. Preliminary expenses represent money spent which has no resale value and are written off over a few years, so they are not real assets. Goodwill and a patent are intangible but real, and furniture is tangible.

questions.stem_md: At the year end an imagined bakery owes wages of ₹7,000, flour suppliers ₹38,000 and rent of ₹5,000. It also has a bank loan of ₹2,00,000 repayable in six years, owner's capital of ₹3,00,000 and a customer's claim of ₹20,000 still undecided in court. What is the total of its current liabilities?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹50,000. Only wages, suppliers and rent fall due within the year: 7,000 + 38,000 + 5,000 = ₹50,000. The option of ₹2,50,000 adds the long-term loan, ₹70,000 adds the undecided claim, which is only contingent, and ₹3,50,000 adds the owner's capital, which is an internal liability.

questions.stem_md: Falgun Fabrics (imagined) has guaranteed a bank loan of ₹80,000 taken by a supplier. The firm will have to pay only if the supplier fails to repay. How should the guarantee be treated in the books of Falgun Fabrics?

options.text_md: Recorded as a current liability of ₹80,000 at once
Not recorded as an actual liability; it is mentioned as a contingent liability
Recorded as a long-term liability of ₹80,000
Added to the owner's capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Not recorded as an actual liability; it is mentioned as a contingent liability. The duty to pay arises only if an uncertain future event happens, so it is not an actual liability today and is only disclosed. Showing it as a current or long-term liability treats it as certain, and capital is unrelated to it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A contingent liability is not recorded as an actual liability in the books.

**Reason (R):** It depends on a future event that may or may not happen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true. Because the payment depends on an uncertain event, there is no present obligation to record, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.stem_md: A coal mine owned by a firm is an example of a wasting asset.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The mine is exhausted as coal is taken out of it, which is the mark of a wasting asset.

questions.stem_md: Preliminary expenses which have not yet been written off are shown in the balance sheet as a ___ asset.
questions.solution_md: They have no resale value and are only a cost awaiting write-off, so they are called a fictitious asset.

questions.stem_md: Koraput Coffee Roasters (imagined) has these balances: roasting machine ₹2,10,000, land ₹3,50,000, stock of coffee beans ₹64,000, debtors ₹38,000, cash in hand ₹22,000, bank balance ₹71,000, preliminary expenses ₹10,000. It owes a bank loan repayable in five years of ₹2,00,000, creditors ₹46,000 and wages ₹8,000. A customer has also claimed ₹30,000 in a case that is pending. Find the owner's capital.
questions.solution_md: The pending claim is only a contingent liability, so it is left out. Capital = assets − external liabilities = 7,65,000 − 2,54,000 = ₹5,11,000.

questions.stem_md: Dharwad Dhaba Supplies (imagined) has cash in hand ₹14,000, a bank balance of ₹86,000, marketable securities of ₹30,000, debtors of ₹45,000, stock of ₹60,000 and furniture of ₹25,000. Take liquid assets to be cash, bank balances and marketable securities. Find its liquid assets.
questions.solution_md: Debtors, stock and furniture are left out. Liquid assets = 14,000 + 86,000 + 30,000 = ₹1,30,000.

questions.stem_md: Total assets of Gadag Gunny Bags (imagined) were ₹5,40,000 and its external liabilities ₹2,10,000 at the start of the year. At the end, assets were ₹6,20,000 and external liabilities ₹2,45,000. By how much did the owner's capital change during the year?
Why is a contingent liability not shown as an actual liability? Give one example.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the reason and one for a correct example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A contingent liability becomes payable only if an uncertain future event happens, so the firm has no present obligation to record, and it is only disclosed by a note.
2. Example: a pending court claim for damages against the firm, or a guarantee given for the loan of another person.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: depends on an uncertain future event

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a **wasting asset** from a **fictitious asset**, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: A mark for each term with its example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **wasting asset** is a real asset that is used up as it is worked, for example a quarry or an oil well.
2. A **fictitious asset** is not a real asset: it is an expense that has not yet been written off, for example preliminary expenses.

questions.stem_md:
Classify each of these items of Jhunjhunu Toy Mart (imagined) as a fixed tangible asset, fixed intangible asset, current asset, fictitious asset, current liability or long-term liability. Choose the most exact class.

(1) A trademark registered by the firm
(2) Cash in the till
(3) A loan from a bank, due in seven years
(4) Goods lying unsold in the shop
(5) Rent due to the landlord
(6) Advertising cost not yet written off
questions.solution_md: Half a mark for each correct class, rounded up to a whole mark at the end; read the time of payment or the form of the asset first.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | Class |
|---|---|
| (1) | Fixed asset, intangible |
| (2) | Current asset (liquid) |
| (3) | Long-term liability |
| (4) | Current asset |
| (5) | Current liability |
| (6) | Fictitious asset |

questions.stem_md: Explain **internal**, **external** and **contingent** liabilities, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each kind, with its example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Internal liability:** owed to the owner of the business, for example capital.
2. **External liability:** owed to outsiders, either current (due within a year, for example creditors) or long-term (due later, for example a bank loan repayable in six years).
3. **Contingent liability:** arises only if an uncertain event happens and is not recorded as a liability; for example, a pending case for damages.

questions.stem_md: Nakhatrana Needle Works (imagined) shows assets of ₹7,60,000 and liabilities to outsiders of ₹2,95,000. A customer's claim of ₹40,000 is pending in court. Find the owner's capital and state why the claim is not deducted.
questions.solution_md: Method note: the contingent item stays outside the equation.

answer.model_answer_md:
Capital = total assets − external liabilities = ₹7,60,000 − ₹2,95,000 = ₹4,65,000.
The claim is a contingent liability: it depends on the decision of the court, so it is not an actual liability and is not deducted.

marking_scheme.step: Reason for leaving out the claim

questions.stem_md:
Ambala Cotton Mills (imagined) has the following balances: factory building ₹6,40,000; goodwill ₹90,000; stock of cotton ₹1,20,000; debtors ₹74,000; cash in hand ₹11,000; bank balance ₹63,000; deferred advertising expenditure ₹20,000; limestone pit ₹1,50,000. It owes a loan from a finance company, due in nine years, of ₹3,00,000, creditors of ₹85,000 and salaries due of ₹12,000.

(a) Name the class (fixed tangible, fixed intangible, current, liquid current, fictitious or wasting) of each of the eight assets. [4]

(b) Find the owner's capital. [1]
questions.solution_md: Two classes earn one mark in part (a); part (b) needs both totals.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Asset | Class | ₹ |
|---|---|---|
| Factory building | Fixed, tangible | 6,40,000 |
| Goodwill | Fixed, intangible | 90,000 |
| Stock of cotton | Current | 1,20,000 |
| Debtors | Current | 74,000 |
| Cash in hand | Current, liquid | 11,000 |
| Bank balance | Current, liquid | 63,000 |
| Deferred advertising expenditure | Fictitious | 20,000 |
| Limestone pit | Wasting | 1,50,000 |

**(b)** Total assets ₹11,68,000 less external liabilities (loan, creditors, salaries due) ₹3,97,000 gives capital ₹7,71,000.

questions.stem_md: In a month, Hosur Valve Works (imagined) sold valves worth ₹40,000 on credit to Aman Dealers, ₹22,000 for cash and ₹15,000 on credit to Sethi Pumps. Aman Dealers paid ₹25,000. The firm also bought a drill on credit for ₹9,000. What is the total owed to the firm by its trade debtors at the end of the month?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹30,000. Trade debtors owe for credit sales less what has been received: 40,000 + 15,000 − 25,000 = ₹30,000. The option of ₹52,000 includes the cash sale, which creates no debtor, ₹55,000 ignores the receipt, and ₹21,000 wrongly sets off the drill, which is owed to its seller and has nothing to do with debtors.

questions.stem_md: At a manufacturing firm, cloth that has been cut and partly stitched into shirts, but is not yet ready for sale, is counted as

options.text_md: raw material
work in progress
finished goods
opening stock of the next year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** work in progress. Partly completed goods are work in progress. The cloth before cutting would be raw material, and finished goods are complete and packed for sale.

questions.stem_md: Goods worth ₹68,000 remain unsold in a shop on the last day of the year. In the next year's books this amount will be the

options.text_md: closing stock
purchases
work in progress
opening stock

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** opening stock. Unsold goods at the end of the year are the closing stock of that year, and the same amount is carried forward as the opening stock of the next year. They are not new purchases and not unfinished goods.

questions.stem_md: Karimnagar Steel Furniture (imagined) owes money to four parties. Which one is NOT a trade creditor?

options.text_md: A machinery dealer from whom a lathe was bought on credit
A steel supplier from whom sheets for resale were bought on credit
A hardware merchant who supplied bolts for manufacture on credit
A paint wholesaler from whom paint for the furniture was bought on credit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A machinery dealer from whom a lathe was bought on credit. Trade creditors supply the goods in which the firm deals or the materials it uses in making them. A lathe is a fixed asset, so its supplier is a creditor for an asset and not a trade creditor.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Work in progress is a kind of finished goods.

**Reason (R):** Work in progress consists of goods which are complete and ready to be sold.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Work in progress is partly made goods that are not yet ready for sale, which is the very opposite of finished goods.

questions.stem_md: A supplier who delivers a delivery van to a trader on credit is a trade creditor of the trader.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The van is a fixed asset and not goods for trading, so the supplier is a creditor for an asset and not a trade creditor.

questions.stem_md: The unsold stock on the last day of one year becomes the ___ stock of the following year.
questions.solution_md: The closing stock of one period is carried forward as the opening stock of the next.

questions.stem_md: Hampi Stone Craft (imagined) began the year with stock of ₹52,000. It bought goods worth ₹3,48,000 and sent back goods worth ₹18,000 to its suppliers. The cost of the goods it sold was ₹3,25,000. Find the closing stock.
questions.solution_md: Closing stock = opening stock + purchases − purchases return − cost of goods sold = 52,000 + 3,48,000 − 18,000 − 3,25,000 = ₹57,000.

questions.stem_md: Kollur Coconut Oil (imagined) had 340 tins in stock at the beginning of the month, bought 1,900 tins and sold 2,060 tins. Each tin costs ₹250. Find the value of the closing stock at cost.
Leh Woollens (imagined) sold goods worth ₹95,000 on credit to Lalit Traders. Goods of ₹5,000 were returned by Lalit Traders, who then paid ₹60,000. How much does Lalit Traders still owe?
Mandla Mat Mills (imagined) bought goods for cash worth ₹1,25,000 and on credit worth ₹2,05,000 during the year, and sent goods worth ₹14,500 back to its suppliers. Find its net purchases.
questions.solution_md: Purchases include both cash and credit buying; the returns are deducted. Net purchases = 1,25,000 + 2,05,000 − 14,500 = ₹3,15,500.

questions.stem_md: Ladakh Apricot Traders (imagined) sold dried apricots for cash worth ₹2,10,000 and on credit worth ₹3,40,000. Customers returned goods worth ₹18,000. Find the net sales for the year.
questions.solution_md: Both kinds of sale count, and the returns are deducted. Net sales = 2,10,000 + 3,40,000 − 18,000 = ₹5,32,000.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a **trade debtor** from a **trade creditor**.
questions.solution_md: A mark for each term with the direction of the debt.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **trade debtor** is a person who owes money to the firm for goods bought from it on credit; to the firm it is an asset.
2. A **trade creditor** is a person to whom the firm owes money for goods bought from him on credit; to the firm it is a liability.

questions.stem_md: Dhule Spice Mill (imagined) grinds whole spices and sells packets. Name the kind of stock, with a reason, for (a) whole chillies in the godown, (b) chillies partly ground and not yet packed, (c) sealed packets waiting for the van.
questions.solution_md: One mark each for the kind and reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Raw material, because the chillies are yet to enter production.
**(b)** Work in progress, because processing has begun but the goods are not complete.
**(c)** Finished goods, because they are complete and ready for sale.

questions.stem_md: Tinsukia Tea Packers (imagined) sold tea worth ₹90,000 on credit to Naresh Stores and bought a packing machine worth ₹24,000 on credit from Orient Machines. It also bought tea worth ₹1,50,000 on credit from Sonari Estates. Naresh Stores has paid ₹35,000; ₹1,00,000 has been paid to Sonari Estates. Name the trade debtor and the trade creditor, and the balance of each.
questions.solution_md: The machine is a fixed asset and stays out of the trade accounts.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Trade debtor:** Naresh Stores owes ₹90,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹55,000.
**Trade creditor:** Sonari Estates is owed ₹1,50,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹50,000.
Orient Machines is owed for a machine, which is an asset, so it is not a trade creditor.

marking_scheme.step: Orient Machines identified as not a trade creditor

questions.stem_md:
Rudrapur Cycle Works (imagined) shows these stocks: raw material ₹1,60,000 at the start and ₹1,75,000 at the end; work in progress ₹24,000 at the start and ₹31,000 at the end; finished goods ₹96,000 at the start and ₹82,000 at the end. It sold goods on credit to Gopal Cycles for ₹70,000, which Gopal paid in part: ₹45,000.

(a) Find the total opening stock and the total closing stock. [2]

(b) State what the closing stock becomes in the next year. [1]

(c) Find the balance of Gopal Cycles and name the account it is called. [2]
questions.solution_md: Add the three kinds of stock separately for each date.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Stock | Start (₹) | End (₹) |
|---|---|---|
| Raw material | 1,60,000 | 1,75,000 |
| Work in progress | 24,000 | 31,000 |
| Finished goods | 96,000 | 82,000 |
| Total | 2,80,000 | 2,88,000 |

**(a)** Opening stock is ₹2,80,000 and closing stock is ₹2,88,000.

**(b)** The closing stock is carried forward as the opening stock of the next year.

**(c)** Gopal Cycles owes ₹70,000 − ₹45,000 = ₹25,000, so it is a trade debtor.

marking_scheme.step: (b) becomes opening stock of the next year

questions.stem_md: Which one of these users of accounting information is an internal user?

options.text_md: A bank that has given the firm a loan
The income-tax department
The manager of the firm
A supplier who sells to the firm on credit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The manager of the firm. Owners, managers and employees work inside the business. The bank, the tax department and the supplier are outsiders.

questions.stem_md: A flour mill (imagined) is asked by a new customer for goods on sixty days of credit. Before agreeing, the mill studies the customer's accounts. What is the mill mainly trying to learn?

options.text_md: How much tax the customer should pay
What bonus the customer's staff should receive
Whether the customer can pay its dues on time
Whether the customer's prices are fair for consumers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Whether the customer can pay its dues on time. A supplier giving credit wants to be sure of payment. Tax, bonus and fair prices are the concerns of the tax authority, employees and consumers.

questions.stem_md: Siliguri Bamboo Furniture (imagined) wants to find the exact cost of making one chair of each design in order to fix selling prices. Which branch of accounting helps?

options.text_md: Cost accounting
Financial accounting
Book-keeping
Auditing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cost accounting. Cost accounting finds and analyses the cost of products and services. Financial accounting reports on the whole business, book-keeping only records, and auditing is an independent examination.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly separates financial accounting from management accounting?

options.text_md: Financial accounting is meant only for managers, and management accounting only for tax officers
Management accounting is compulsory by law, but financial accounting is not
Financial accounting deals only with the future, and management accounting only with the past
Financial accounting reports on the whole business, mainly to outsiders, in a standard form; management accounting serves managers and has no fixed form

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Financial accounting reports on the whole business, mainly to outsiders, in a standard form; management accounting serves managers and has no fixed form. Financial accounting reports past results of the whole firm to owners and outsiders in an accepted form, whereas management accounting is designed for managers and may look to the future. The other statements swap the users, the legal position or the time reference.

questions.stem_md: Match each user of the accounts of a milk cooperative (imagined) with what the user mainly wants to learn.

options.text_md: A bank considering a loan
The tax department
The staff of the dairy
A researcher

match_right.text_md: Facts and trends of the dairy trade for a study
Whether interest and the loan can be repaid
Whether wages and bonus can be paid and jobs are safe
The profit on which tax is payable

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each user asks the question that fits its own decision.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The income-tax authorities are external users of the accounts of a firm.

**Reason (R):** Government departments want the profit figure of a firm in order to assess the tax due.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. The reason describes what tax authorities need, but they are external because they stand outside the business, which the reason does not explain.

questions.stem_md: The branch of accounting that gives managers information for planning, control and decision making is called ___ accounting.
questions.solution_md: Management accounting is meant for the managers inside the firm.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish **internal users** from **external users** of accounting information, with two examples of each.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each group with two correct examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Internal users** own, manage or work in the business, for example the owners and the managers.
2. **External users** are outside the business and deal with it, for example banks and tax authorities.

questions.stem_md: State **two** differences between cost accounting and management accounting.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct differences earn a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Scope:** cost accounting is concerned with the cost of products, jobs and services; management accounting uses cost and other facts across the whole business.
2. **Purpose:** cost accounting helps to control and reduce costs; management accounting helps managers to plan, control and take decisions.

questions.stem_md: Arunachal Orange Growers (imagined) is applying for a bank loan to build a juice plant, offers a bonus to its staff and files a tax return. Name the user in each situation and say what that user wants from the accounts.
questions.solution_md: Each user and its need earns one mark.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The bank** (external): the ability of the firm to pay interest and repay the loan.
2. **The staff** (internal): whether the firm can pay the bonus and keep them in employment.
3. **The tax authority** (external): the profit of the year, on which the tax is assessed.

questions.stem_md: Compare financial, cost and management accounting by their main purpose.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the purpose of each branch.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Financial accounting:** records transactions of the whole business and reports profit or loss and financial position, chiefly for owners and outsiders.
2. **Cost accounting:** finds and analyses the cost of products, jobs or services so that costs can be controlled.
3. **Management accounting:** presents information, in any useful form, to managers for planning, control and decisions.

questions.stem_md:
Tawang Yak Wool Weavers (imagined) is owned by Dorjee and run by a manager, with twelve employees. It buys wool on credit from herders, has a bank loan and sells to a retail chain.

Name **five** users of its accounts and state, in one line each, what each user wants to know from them.
questions.solution_md: Any five users, each linked to a distinct need, one mark each; naming a user without its need earns nothing.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Owner (Dorjee), internal:** the profit earned and whether his capital is safe.
2. **Manager, internal:** detailed figures about costs and sales to plan and control the work.
3. **Employees, internal:** whether wages and bonus can be paid and their jobs are secure.
4. **Bank, external:** whether interest can be paid and the loan repaid on time.
5. **Wool suppliers on credit, external:** whether the firm can pay for the wool it has bought.
6. **Tax authority, external:** the profit, so that tax can be fixed.

questions.stem_md:
Cuttack Cycle Components (imagined) makes bicycle parts. Its owner wants its yearly profit and position reported to the bank, the foreman wants to know why the cost of a hub rose, and the director wants help in deciding whether to add a second shift.

(a) Name the branch of accounting that serves each of the three needs. [3]

(b) Distinguish financial accounting from cost accounting on two points. [2]
questions.solution_md: Match each need to the work done before comparing the branches.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The report to the bank is financial accounting; the rise in the cost of a hub is cost accounting; the decision on the second shift is management accounting.
**(b)** 1. Financial accounting reports on the whole business for outsiders and owners; cost accounting concentrates on the cost of products and services.
2. Financial accounting follows accepted principles and gives results of a period; cost accounting gives detailed information to managers during the work, for control.

marking_scheme.step: (a) cost of a hub: cost accounting
